summary: New rule: one- and two-family dwellings need an outdoor, readily accessible emergency disconnect for first responders; the service disconnect, a meter disconnect, or other listed supply-side disconnect can serve. Parallel outdoor-disconnect rules were added for generators, ESS, storage batteries and wind systems.

New rule: services supplying dwelling units must have a Type 1 or Type 2 SPD, integral to or adjacent to service equipment (or at next downstream distribution equipment); also applies when service equipment is replaced.
Dwelling GFCI requirements now cover receptacles rated 125 V through 250 V in the listed locations (pulls in 240 V receptacles such as dryer/range outlets in covered areas).
GFCI now required for receptacles in all dwelling basements, finished or unfinished (previously only unfinished).

New: dwelling outdoor outlets (not just receptacles) up to 50 A and 150 V to ground need GFCI, which reaches hardwired equipment such as outdoor HVAC condensers; limited exceptions (e.g., certain lighting/deicing).
notes: Many jurisdictions later amended or delayed this for HVAC; see 2026 Class C SPGFCI exception and Texas 2026 adoption exception.

summary: Doors/doorways no longer count as obstructions when measuring the 6 ft distance to sinks etc., so more receptacles may fall in GFCI zones.
Required count switches to area-based: one receptacle for the first 9 sq ft of island/peninsula countertop and one per additional 18 sq ft; peninsula receptacle within 2 ft of outer end.
Up to six service disconnects may no longer be grouped in a single enclosure without separation, to allow an electrically safe condition when one is opened.
The single-phase dwelling service/feeder ampacity method (83% rule) moved from an informative annex into enforceable Article 310 text.
Ceiling outlet boxes in habitable rooms where a fan could be installed must be listed for fan support regardless of the presence of a spare conductor.
Receptacles prohibited within a zone 3 ft horizontally and 8 ft vertically from tub/shower thresholds; small-bathroom exception for far wall.
Further expansion of GFCI: dwelling kitchen receptacles broadly, outdoor outlets, certain appliances (422.5), plus other-than-dwelling areas such as commercial food prep; new exceptions.
SPD requirement extended to more occupancy types (e.g., dormitories, guest rooms, patient sleeping rooms), applies to service replacement, and SPD must have at least 10 kA nominal discharge rating.
New SPD requirements for feeders and outside feeders, modeled on 230.67, for the same occupancy list; SPD in or adjacent to feeder-supplied distribution equipment.
notes: Stated in MN DLI 2026 NEC FAQ item 8 as having been added in the 2023 NEC.

summary: AFCI requirements reorganized into (A)-(E) and extended to sleeping quarters in fire/police stations and nursing homes; 10 A circuits addressed.
Receptacle on islands/peninsulas becomes optional, but a raceway or cable must be provided to a covered box for a future receptacle if none is installed.
Receptacles installed below countertop surfaces are prohibited (with a USB-device-related allowance per IAEI); section number not given by source.
New 10 A branch circuit permitted for limited loads (fixed lighting, exhaust fans, gas fireplace), not for general-use receptacles. IAEI cites 210.18; verify exact section.
Rules for reconditioned equipment: some devices may not be reconditioned; breakers/switchgear may be if marked and traceable, with listing/field-labeling/AHJ paths.
Working-space height clarified (6.5 ft or equipment top, whichever greater); open equipment doors may not reduce egress below 24 in.
All definitions moved into Article 100 (start of code reorganization).
New/restructured articles for systems over 1000 V AC / 1500 V DC.

Article 690 scope covers stand-alone/hybrid/grid-tied PV with 691 for large-scale; floating PV; rapid shutdown exception for detached non-enclosed structures (carports); updated terminology for 705/706/710.
Electric pool heater element/OCPD limits; pool equipment rooms need drainage and a GFCI-protected receptacle.

2026 NEC issued by NFPA Standards Council 2025-08-20, effective (available for adoption) 2025-09-09. NFPA map (as of 2026-08-03) lists 2026 in force in CO, ME, MA, MN, ND, WY; since then Texas (eff. 2026-09-01) and Oregon OESC (eff. 2026-10-01) verified on official pages; Washington expected 2026-12-31.
Clarifies that following manufacturer installation instructions must still produce a code-compliant installation; instructions cannot override NEC.

(A)/(B) combined, generic warning and 1000 A threshold removed; labels for other-than-dwelling equipment must give nominal voltage, arc-flash boundary, incident energy or PPE category, and assessment date. MN does not require it on dwelling accessory structures but does on temporary services.
Garages split into their own list item and the at-or-below-grade qualifier removed; accessory buildings limited to storage/work areas in item (3). Habitable spaces in/above garages are not covered.

New exception allows Class C SPGFCI protection for listed HVAC equipment (MN: after 2026-09-01) with a required disconnect marking. MN will not enforce GFCI on like-for-like replacement of existing HVAC/disconnect where circuit unaltered (state statute).
notes: Texas 2026 adoption also includes a limited exception for certain outdoor-outlet GFCI requirements.

summary: An outlet branch-circuit AFCI may now be placed at the first receptacle outlet or switch of the existing branch circuit when wiring is modified/replaced/extended.
All fixed cabinets are excluded from receptacle wall-space measurement (previously only those without countertops).
Receptacle outlets may not be within 24 in. beneath or adjacent to countertops/work surfaces; new exception for hardwired receptacles in drawers.

SPD scope (services and feeders) covers new and replacement distribution equipment in dwellings, dormitories, hotel guest rooms, patient sleeping rooms, and emergency-service sleeping quarters; Type 1 or 2, In >= 10 kA. MN guidance covers pole-mounted disconnects, farm panels, single-equipment disconnects.
Feeder disconnect for a building: if outside, readily accessible on or within sight of the building; if inside, nearest point of entrance of feeder conductors.

230.85 emergency disconnect deleted and folded into 230.70: one- and two-family dwelling service disconnect must be outdoors, readily accessible, on or within sight of the dwelling. Utility-provided disconnects generally will not count unless they comply with 230.70.
GEC splices permitted with listed grounding/bonding equipment at accessible locations, in addition to exothermic and irreversible compression.
New text: conductors/wiring methods made unsuitable by damage (heat, fire, corrosion, water) must be replaced; NEMA GD 1/GD 2 referenced as guidance.
Clarifies ceiling boxes in typical fan locations in dwelling living/sleeping areas must be listed for fan support or allow direct access to structural framing.
NM cable without 15-minute thermal barrier allowed in non-habitable grade-level storage garages/buildings under 1500 sq ft.

Aircraft hangar underground wiring no longer Class I Div 1 (seals required); fuel dispenser emergency disconnect must also kill nearby receptacles; equipotential plane construction details added (547, 555, 682); pool perimeter bonding depth increased from 2 ft to 3 ft below max water level and single #8 often no longer enough; fire pump feeder interior encasement increased from 2 in. to 5 in. concrete.
